Pitchwise Holdings, a consortium of family offices and long-term institutional investors led by sports executives Ann Rodriguez and Corey Woolfolk, will acquire the shares from majority owner Meriton Holdings, Valencia said. The investors will also inject €100 million into the club, Valencia said, adding that the deal remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. Meriton will retain a majority stake, while Kiat Lim will remain president. Rodriguez and Woolfolk will join Lim in a new ownership group, Valencia said. The deal comes as wealthy families and institutional investors [USN:L4N43E020 TEXT:"increasingly seek exposure"] to sports franchises, attracted by their global audiences, media rights and commercial growth potential. Pitchwise's backers include Roberts and Kravis, co-founders and co-executive chairmen of KKR, the global investment firm, as well as Penner Sports Group, the Denver-based sports and entertainment holding company founded by Greg and Carrie Penner. Penner Sports Group's holdings include the NFL's Denver Broncos and a minority stake in Major League Baseball's Colorado Rockies, Valencia said. Lim said Pitchwise was selected from several interested parties because of its "long-term investment expertise and sports acumen". Valencia said the valuation reflects its men's and women's teams, the 49,000-seat Mestalla stadium and [USN:L4N3SS0RP TEXT:"the Nou Mestalla project"], which is expected to have capacity for more than 70,000 fans. The new ownership group will oversee the club's move to the Nou Mestalla stadium, which Valencia described as its most significant milestone in 100 years. ($1 = 0.8937 euros)

item.title: Seven killed as gunmen open fire at church in Jordan in 'terrorist' attack, authorities say
item.description: The gunmen started shooting during a funeral procession, in a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority that authorities described as a terrorist act by extremists.
item.dc:creator: Alaa al-Sukhni
item.content:encoded: Seven people were killed on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, said the head of the country's Public Security Directorate, in a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority that authorities described as a terrorist act by extremists. Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded. Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US ally say that in recent years they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by Islamist militants. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. A video aired on Jordan's state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details. "This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path," Jordanian Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said in a post on X. Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes. Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse on the floor after the attack. "People were crying, wailing, screaming — it's hard to describe," he said. BLOOD SMEARED ON THE GROUND Jordan's King Abdullah, a major US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist". "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement. Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed. In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable. People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock. "What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas — where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen. Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. The US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship." Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

item.title: Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week
item.description: Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi, Ragini Mathur
item.content:encoded: Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting. The Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending. The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35% gain on Friday. Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector. [USN:L6N46811D TEXT:"Next week"], about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) , three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street. "There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. "There's certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data center build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that's giving pause." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34. For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain. [USN:L4N4691CQ TEXT:"Telecommunications stocks fell"], weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX (SPCX.O) was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier. Shares of AT&T (T.N) and T-Mobile (TMUS.O) both sank nearly 8% while Verizon (VZ.N) shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle (CCI.N) up 9% and American Tower (AMT.N) up 4%. The energy sector (.SPNY) rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East. American Express (AXP.N) shares fell 3.7%, weighing on the Dow. [USN:L4N4690T1 TEXT:"The company raised its profit forecast"] as it also announced plans to eliminate 5% of its workforce. SLB (SLB.N) shares rose 7% after the oilfield services provider [USN:L4N4690VH TEXT:"beat Wall Street estimates"] for third-quarter profit. Data from the University of Michigan showed [USN:AQN2MPKQ5 TEXT:"US consumer sentiment edged down"] near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy. Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting. Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the November 3 midterm elections , which will decide control of the US Congress. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq, declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.57-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 18 new 52-week highs and 8 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 74 new highs and 334 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 15.4 billion shares, compared with the 17.2 billion average over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: France spared Moody's ratings downgrade as it struggles with unrest
item.description: Moody's spared France a credit rating downgrade on Friday, easing pressure on a government struggling to contain social unrest and shore up its strained finances.
item.dc:creator: Leigh Thomas, Dhara Ranasinghe
item.content:encoded: Moody's spared France a credit rating downgrade on Friday, easing pressure on a government struggling to contain social unrest and shore up its strained finances. Moody's said it had concluded a periodic review of its rating, leaving it at Aa3, which has carried a negative outlook since last October. Bond markets had been pricing in a downgrade, which would have brought Moody's in line with Standard & Poor's and Fitch, which moved earlier as France struggled to rein in its public finances after a 2024 snap election produced a hung parliament and political paralysis. The French finance ministry said in a statement that the fact Moody's kept its rating unchanged reflected the "credibility of the budget the government has put forward in the 2027 finance bill, which is designed to keep our public finances on the path to recovery." The government is struggling to pass the bill in parliament, where opposition parties could refuse to compromise, reject the legislation and topple the government in a no-confidence vote. "The Aa3 rating assumes that a deficit-reducing budget for 2027 will be adopted, while financing costs and social tensions will abate somewhat in the next few months," Moody's said in a statement. French borrowing costs already exceed those of [USN:L6N468116 TEXT:"lower-rated peers"] such as Italy, as investors fret over the budget deficit — one of the euro zone's biggest — and a presidential election on April 18 and May 2 next year that polls suggest the far right could win. TV images of [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"weekend protests"] descending into riots and looting underscore the political difficulty of pushing budget cuts through. That helped push the [USN:L6N46814J TEXT:"risk premium"] on French government debt over safe-haven German bonds to its highest in 15 years on Thursday, while France's benchmark 10-year bond yield hit 5.14%, its highest level since July 2002. OUTLOOK IN FOCUS Moody's said [USN:B5N44300T TEXT:"earlier this month"] that the French government's ability to overcome "fragmentation in parliament" would be the key factor for its next rating move. That task looks harder after violent protests over underfunded schools escalated last weekend into riots during mass cost-of-living demonstrations. The government has refused to release more school funding or raise the minimum wage, and [USN:L1N46908B TEXT:"further protests"] are planned for Saturday. In parliament, the lower house has scrapped some key savings measures in the 2027 budget, which targets a deficit of 5% of output versus 5.4% this year. Opposition parties show little appetite for compromise before the election, scrapping some proposed cuts while adding spending. "You want to wait and see how the narrative evolves over the next six months into the election. That's going to have a more meaningful impact on the spread," said Rushabh Amin, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments. Pressure on French debt could grow after the presidential vote if Moody's, S&P and Fitch all cut France to BBB — just above junk status — potentially forcing sales by those investors with rating limits, said Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management. "That's where it could really start to get more ugly," he added.

item.content:encoded: Canada’s main stock index added to its weekly decline on Friday as losses for financials and consumer-related stocks offset gains for energy, with recent turbulence globally in AI-linked stocks keeping risk appetite in check. "It's probably been held up by the energy sector but we're starting to see some weakness in banks and some other parts of the market this week." Heavily weighted financials (.SPTTFS) fell 0.9% on Friday, with shares of Manulife Financial Corporation (MFC.TO) down 2.9%. Food and pharmacy retailer Loblaws Companies (L.TO) lost 2.8%, contributing to a 2.2% decline for consumer staples. The materials sector (.GSPTTMT) , which includes metal mining shares, fell 1.2% as gold hit a three-month low ahead of a Federal Reserve interest rate decision next week. The [USN:L6N46911N TEXT:"Bank of Canada"] is also due to make an interest rate decision next week. The majority of economists polled by Reuters expect the central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% and follow with one more hike by the end of March. Telecom operator [USN:L8N4691GI TEXT:"Rogers Communications"] reported third-quarter profit above estimates. Still, its shares were down 2.3%. [USN:L6N469125 TEXT:"US crude oil futures"] settled 3.8% higher at $103.27 a barrel after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East. US President Donald Trump signed an order to [USN:L6N46914T TEXT:"remove 50% tariffs"] on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products.

item.title: Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears
item.description: With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel.
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Renshaw, Leah Douglas
item.content:encoded: With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel. His administration has offered billions of dollars to farmers, relaxed rules for truckers, [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"eased sanctions"] on Russian fuel and pressured European allies to release emergency stocks. Yet diesel prices rose again last week, leaving Trump spending political and financial capital without delivering the relief his party wants as voters go to the polls. Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress, and high costs are a major concern for voters. Nearly 80% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame"] Trump for higher costs, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. US diesel prices [USN:L6N45Z19G TEXT:"rose nearly 10 cents a gallon"] in the latest week to an average of $6.28, reversing two weeks of declines and remaining near record highs, according to the Energy Information Administration. Diesel in the last two months has become a central issue not only in the midterms but as a catalyst driving up already-elevated US inflation. The fuel is critical for farmers, construction companies, freight operators and more, and government data last week showed its rise was partly behind hefty increases in delivery costs, early-stage food production costs and [USN:L6N461198 TEXT:"even toy prices"]. The political pressure is particularly acute in traditionally Republican Farm Belt states like [USN:L6N44F10S TEXT:"Iowa"] and [USN:L6N45F193 TEXT:"Kansas"], where rising fuel and fertilizer costs, trade disruptions and weak farm economics have fueled discontent among some of Trump's core supporters. Trump has promoted his diesel measures at campaign [USN:L1N45Q06H TEXT:"rallies"] across the region. He signed an executive order onstage in Nebraska allowing red-dyed diesel to be used in highway vehicles and announced $8 billion in new farm aid during a rally in Kansas on Monday. The measures illustrate the trade-offs Trump is accepting in pursuit of near-term relief. The new aid adds fresh strain on federal spending, while the Russian fuel move risks helping Moscow finance its war in Ukraine. Pressure on European allies to release emergency stocks, backed by a threat to restrict US diesel exports, has created diplomatic friction. “The president tends to discount long-term losses over short-term gain, and I am skeptical if there is any short gain to be had here,” said Chris Borick, a pollster and political scientist at Muhlenberg College in Pennsylvania. The White House attributed high diesel prices to “pre-existing issues,” including years of refinery closures and damage from Russia's war in Ukraine, while defending Trump's efforts to ease costs. “The President wants diesel prices to fall, which is why he has taken historic actions to save American farmers, truckers, and workers every hard-earned penny," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said. SKEPTICISM AND UNANSWERED QUESTIONS One of Trump's most direct attempts to lower diesel costs has struggled to gain traction. Trump signed an executive order this month [USN:L1N461138 TEXT:"allowing truckers to use red-dyed diesel"], typically intended for off-road use such as farm equipment, for highway driving while temporarily avoiding certain federal tax reporting and record-keeping requirements. But the IRS has not eliminated the federal diesel tax, instead temporarily waiving related reporting requirements and penalties through year-end, leaving uncertainty for truck stops and fuel sellers. David Fialkov, top lobbyist at NATSO, a trade group representing the largest US truck stop operators, said members appreciate Trump's effort to tackle diesel costs but that the guidance remains "murky" and carries too much risk. "I really don’t see any of these dyed diesel announcements making a meaningful dent in diesel prices," Fialkov said. Trump is also turning to federal payments to cushion some of the constituencies feeling the pain. Government payments to farmers were already expected to top $47 billion this year, buoyed by commodity payments and $12 billion in tariff relief [USN:S0N3VI02L TEXT:"distributed "]by the US Department of Agriculture earlier this year. The $8 billion farm relief program would push the total to a record $55.4 billion, exceeding the previous high of $45 billion in 2020, when farmers received pandemic assistance. The payments can help farmers manage higher costs and lost sales but do not directly address the market disruptions driving up fuel and fertilizer prices. They also raise questions about taxpayer spending to compensate producers for damage that farm groups say is linked partly to the administration’s own trade and foreign policies. “This is the second round of emergency aid this year to address losses that were largely foreseeable,” National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said. “Trade disruptions and rising fuel costs tied to conflict abroad have put family farmers in a difficult position, and one-time payments can't provide the stability they need to plan for the future.” The aid will arrive after the November 3 election, and likely not reach farmers until the end of the year, USDA official Richard Fordyce [USN:L6N4690W3 TEXT:"told Reuters"] on Friday. FRICTION OVER RUSSIAN FUEL Some of Trump's efforts to increase diesel supplies carry geopolitical trade-offs. His decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel that were designed to restrict Moscow’s energy revenues and limit its ability to finance its war in Ukraine has [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"drawn bipartisan criticism"] -- and raised questions about whether the move will meaningfully lower US fuel prices. Trump has defended the sanctions relief as necessary to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and to release American prisoner Stephen Hubbard. As the administration's intervention efforts have failed to lower fuel costs, Trump has sought to shift blame toward Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskiy rather than the Iran war ahead of the elections. Analysts say the Iran conflict has been the much bigger driver of the diesel price spike, disrupting global oil flows and refined-fuel supplies, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have helped tighten supplies but played a more limited role in the price. “I sort of see it as a blame-shifting kind of scapegoating operation, more than a genuine attempt to moderate prices in the lead-up to the election,” said Edward Fishman, director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center at the Council on Foreign Relations.

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead Earnings flood, Fed meeting will test rickety AI market rally
item.description: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally. Weakness in technology shares left investors [USN:L6N468196 TEXT:"on edge about the state of the AI trade"] that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary. The Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) posted a slim loss on Friday, a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest daily drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta (META.O) and Lam Research (LRCX.O) . Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners. Three other hyperscalers -- Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) -- headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets. "There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro. "Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain." Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index (.SPX) up 11% in 2026. HYPERSCALERS ON THE HOT SEAT Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32% from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season. "I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings." Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs. "Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management. FED EXPECTED TO PAUSE ON RATES, FOR NOW Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel (INTC.O) and Sandisk (SNDK.O) also could influence the AI trade. Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly (LLY.N) , oil majors Exxon (XOM.N) and Chevron (CVX.N) and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar (CAT.N) . The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than 10% chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data. One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections. However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting a roughly 80% probability of such a move then. Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision. "Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike," Todd said.

item.title: AI-discovered bugs may soon trigger fresh disruptions, cyber experts say
item.description: Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of the outages that percolated across global government websites this week.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, A.J. Vicens
item.content:encoded: Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of [USN:FWN4661WD TEXT:"the outages that percolated"] across global government websites this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to Reuters. AI helped drive a doubling of the number of digital flaws discovered year-on-year, according to research due to be published in the coming days by VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm. Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the digital infrastructure firm Cloudflare (NET.N) , told Reuters he was aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software” and predicted busy months ahead as AI surfaced long-hidden weaknesses in the fabric of the internet. “I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince said in an interview on Thursday. The outages that spread across government sites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on Wednesday happened after the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a venerable programming language that powers a huge swath of the internet. Operators have been rushing to fix their software in anticipation of mass exploitation and, because some felt they could not patch before hackers jumped in, a subset simply [USN:L4N46716K TEXT:"yanked their sites offline"] until they could make them safe. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble to fix PHP came during an already busy week in cybersecurity. The week also brought disclosures of vulnerabilities PHP alternative Node.js and streaming program Plex, breaches tied to AI gateway LiteLLM and development platform Railway, and the revelation that the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had used [USN:L6N4680UW TEXT:"an extraordinarily flimsy cryptographic key"] that potentially put users across the internet at risk. “If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more,” Garrity said. “I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed.” TIMELINES SHORTENING The codebases that run modern programs are sprawling and mistakes, or “bugs,” that open up potential avenues for exploitation often crop up in unexpected places. Previously, finding bugs required a baseline level of skill, and taking advantage of those bugs to build digital lockpicks – called “exploits” – could be expected to take weeks or months of work by an experienced professional. That would in the past have provided defenders a little breathing room to fix bugs and gently roll out software updates. AI has effectively thrown those assumptions [USN:L6N42I12G TEXT:"out the window"]. Models can find one bug after another by subjecting codebases to round-the-clock scrutiny, and can turn around exploits in hours. Shane Fry, the chief technology officer of Virginia-based RunSafe Security, said the demonstrated performance of AI models over the past few months had effectively laid to rest any doubts over whether they would change the industry. “What's fundamentally, and unquestionably, changing is the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponize them,” Fry said. SCARY MONSTERS While all the experts Reuters spoke to agreed that defenders’ timelines were getting shorter, they were split on whether AI would lead to a hacker free-for-all. Daniel Stenberg, the lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argued the vulnerabilities found by AI models tended to be exotic bugs that were difficult for rogue actors to take advantage of. Ramy Rahman, a senior principal solutions engineer at cybersecurity company ArmorCode, said “more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks." There was tentative evidence of that around the PHP vulnerability that drew worldwide concern this week. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io said that – like Amazon (AMZN.O) and Cloudflare – it had seen aggressive attempts to take advantage of the bug. But the firm’s head of research, Esteban Borges, said that, as of 2 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday (1800 GMT), the cybercriminals he tracked appeared to have failed to cobble together a working tool to take advantage of it. Prince, of Cloudflare, told Reuters he had seen anecdotal evidence of compromises linked to the PHP vulnerability. The deluge of AI-driven discoveries might rattle the industry, but would be a net positive in the end, he said, comparing it to slaying the monsters in a haunted house. The confrontation might be scary, he said, but leaving the monsters to lurk quietly behind closed doors was far worse. “The reality is, we’re going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up,” he said.

item.title: Weight-loss drugs fuel protein boom, but with more consumer scrutiny
item.description: Even as consumers seek out new sources of protein for their diets, they are becoming more skeptical of foods advertised as high-protein.
item.dc:creator: Waylon Cunningham, Nicholas Brown
item.content:encoded: Protein-infused bottled water. Ice cream. Boxed macaroni and cheese. Even vodka. The rise of weight-loss drugs is driving a boom in protein-based products, as users of GLP-1 medication like Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) Ozempic and Eli Lilly's (LLY.N) Mounjaro look for ways to counter the muscle loss those drugs can cause. GLP-1 users say they will spend 11% more on high-protein foods than before starting the drugs, according to an August survey from Boston Consulting Group. This is the fifth story in a five-part Reuters series on how weight-loss drugs are changing the way people shop and eat, and how companies are responding to the trend. Even as consumers seek out new sources of protein for their diets, they are becoming more skeptical of foods advertised as high-protein, Reuters interviews with consumers and company executives found. Some shoppers question whether products contain as much protein as advertising implies, while blanching at those that pack in so many additives or sugar that they undercut the health pitch. A report from marketing research firm NielsenIQ earlier this year said the snack industry has entered its "accountability era," noting that 25% of its survey respondents this year said they are using scanning apps to check the nutritional value of products, up from around 17% last year. "Protein is no longer a differentiator," said Chris Costagli, a lead marketing researcher at NielsenIQ, who co-wrote the report. Megan Gisela Bautista, a nonprofit employee in Maryland who does strength training, was recently disappointed by the protein content of a chicken jerky snack that touted high protein in a large, colorful font. "I'd have to eat five of them," Bautista said. "That's bad for you." Zack Spears of Dallas said he is checking nutritional labels regularly, and now watches YouTube videos from an online content creator who reviews protein-marketed products. "As this protein craze pops off, and things are getting more expensive, I want to be sure what I'm putting in my body is healthy," Spears said. Some brands acknowledge the growing consumer scrutiny. “Protein is here to stay, but the conversation must evolve,” said Susan Zaripheh, North America chief research officer for yogurt maker Danone (DANO.PA) , in a statement to Reuters. “Consumers are starting to look ‘beyond the gram,’ becoming more informed in the nuances of protein source and nutrient density.” Over the summer, the French food company filed a false advertising [USN:L6N42P17H TEXT:"lawsuit"] against rival yogurt maker Chobani, accusing it of inflating its protein claims on labels by using non-standard serving sizes. Chobani has disputed those claims, telling Reuters in a statement that its labeling is accurate and transparent. Zaripheh said consumers want products that also aid in digestibility and contain other nutrients like fiber. In addition to existing high-protein yogurts and soy milks, the company is developing products that combine protein with other nutrients. Globe Market Research estimated over the summer that the worldwide protein-enriched food market was worth nearly $58 billion last year. But Hormel Foods (HRL.N) , well-known for protein-heavy products like Spam and canned lunch meats, said it is avoiding the use of additives to increase protein in its products. "We believe that in the long run, people don't want too much science in their food," said Jason Levine, Hormel chief marketing officer, referring to additives like "whey powder or pea powder or scientifically engineered protein isolates." SCRUTINIZING LABELS Reuters found several brands that advertise protein content based on a larger portion size than used in regular versions of the same product, including in pastas, oatmeals and granolas. Nature Valley, a snack brand owned by General Mills (GIS.N) , sells a version of its “oats ‘n honey” loose granola that advertises 13 grams of protein on its packaging, based on a 2/3 cup (65 grams) serving size, more than twice as big as the 1/4 cup (27 grams) it calls a serving size for its regular, non-enhanced granola. General Mills, in a statement, said it considers the regular version a snack while the protein version can be eaten either as a snack or a more complete cereal meal. The product's protein-to-calorie ratio, a metric dietitians use to describe a product's protein content, indicates a “very low amount of protein overall,” said Jonathan Bonnet, a Stanford professor and chief medical officer at the Ardmore Institute of Health, adding that a glass of skim milk has more protein than the 2/3-cup serving. Bonnet said more patients are asking him lately for guidance on their protein intake. Still, other companies are expanding their offerings to meet demand. Researcher Circana reported in August that around 48% of US adults are looking to add protein in their diets, up 7 points from last year. Discount supermarket chain Aldi recently told Reuters it is launching a new line of private-label protein pancakes in October, the latest in a string of high-protein items released this year that have included sparkling water, crackers and wagyu beef jerky. Walmart will start selling a new, protein-infused instant coffee product from J.M. Smucker's (SJM.N) Folgers from November until January exclusively, Walmart told Reuters last month. Some consumers and dietitians say the protein trend has led people to eat more protein than they need. NielsenIQ's report said a third of more than 1,000 surveyed respondents believe the food industry is overhyping protein — and another third believe some products have too much protein. Dana Hunnes, a professor and clinical dietitian at UCLA, says the average person doesn't need as much protein as industry marketing has promoted. And some protein-marketed products have too many processed ingredients to qualify as healthy, Hunnes said. “I’ve seen the equivalent of a candy bar” advertising protein, she said. “Just because it has protein doesn’t mean it’s something you should eat." item.title: Take Five: AI trade meets the Fed
item.description: An eye-catching week is in store as rate-setters at the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan announce policy decisions, while investors will gauge whether results from Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft can fuel the next leg of the AI rally.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An eye-catching week is in store as rate-setters at the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan announce policy decisions, while investors will gauge whether results from Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft can fuel the next leg of the AI rally. Elections in Israel and Brazil, a gathering of China's top leadership and a closely watched British budget add political risk to the agenda. Here's all you need to know about the coming week in financial markets by Lewis Krauskopf in New York, Kevin Buckland in Tokyo, and Dhara Ranasinghe, Marc Jones and William Schomberg in London. 1/ MOVE OVER It's a packed week for central banks. The Fed, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of New Zealand meet on Wednesday, the ECB on Thursday, and the [USN:L4N4650G0 TEXT:"BOJ"] a day later. The Fed, ECB and BOJ face no immediate pressure to hike rates after tightening last month. Fed Chair [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"Kevin Warsh"] will be pressed on his view on the rate outlook. The ECB is sure to face questions about surging [USN:L8N4670MT TEXT:"French borrowing costs"] that risk becoming a flashpoint, while the BOJ may [USN:L4N4650KC TEXT:"raise its inflation forecasts"] in a post-meeting report. Markets expect Canada and [USN:L6N4671E0 TEXT:"New Zealand"] to hike rates to contain inflation, with all policymakers grappling with the extent to which high oil will fuel broader price pressures. 2/ HYPERSCALER HOT SEAT A big week for US [USN:L6N45T17Q TEXT:"corporate earnings"] will be headlined by reports from three of the largest companies at the heart of the huge AI capital investment theme that has driven up equities. Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) — three of the so-called hyperscalers — will post results at a time investors are becoming wary of the [USN:L6N45Y119 TEXT:"risks"] of the spending on data centres. The week will be critical to determining if the third quarter lived up to high expectations for US profit growth, with about one-third of S&P 500 (.SPX) companies reporting. Other high-profile firms set to report include drugmaker Eli Lilly (LLY.N) , oil majors Exxon (XOM.N) and Chevron (CVX.N) , and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar (CAT.N) . 3/ FISCAL TIGHTROPE British finance minister John Healey will announce his first budget on Wednesday, when he will try to offer some relief from higher [USN:L6N45O0SR TEXT:"energy prices"] to households, but without unsettling the bond market by ramping up [USN:L8N46708T TEXT:"borrowing"]. That means Healey may have to accept a narrowing of his room for manoeuvre to meet his fiscal rules. Analysts polled by Reuters think he can allow his headroom to almost halve to around £15 billion ($20 billion) without spooking the market. [USN:L1N46206Z TEXT:"Banks"] might bear the brunt of tax increases, and the share prices of Britain's biggest lenders have fallen in the run-up to Healey's high-profile debut. Bigger decisions on spending in areas such as defence, public services and welfare are likely to be put off until next year, with Healey hoping the Iran war — and the pressure it is putting on government borrowing costs — may have abated by then. 4/ NETANYAHU'S MOMENT OF TRUTH Israel's [USN:L8N3XX04M TEXT:"election"] on Tuesday is poised to be one of the most consequential in the country's history. Polls have it as a coin toss , with neither Prime Minister [USN:L1N45L0EX TEXT:"Benjamin Netanyahu's"] Likud bloc nor an opposition centred around former military chief Gadi Eisenkot expected to win a majority, raising the prospect of lengthy coalition negotiations. Yet for markets, it also comes after an [USN:L8N46801Y TEXT:"extraordinary rally"] in Israeli assets. Since 2023's October 7 attacks, the Tel Aviv stock market (.TA125) has surged more than 135%, while the shekel is up a world-beating 25%. Analysts are quick to point out the AI boom has been key, given Israel's tech expertise, and will remain so. But investors also see the potential for tensions to be gradually dialled down in the longer term if Eisenkot and his allies can win out. In Brazil, the presidential election will reach its conclusion on Sunday, with markets hoping Flavio Bolsonaro can edge out current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva after the challenger's surprisingly strong first-round performance sent stocks surging to a [USN:L1N45R06Y TEXT:"record high"]. 5/ PARTY PRIORITIES China's top [USN:L6N4680FF TEXT:"leadership"] gathers in Beijing for the four-day [USN:L1N45D08Z TEXT:"Fifth Plenum"] from Monday, with officials deliberating on "Advancing Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance." That may sound inward-looking, but official Chinese commentary frames the initiative as an effort to strengthen Party discipline and execution in response to a more challenging external environment, including an increasingly tense relationship with the [USN:L8N45K07F TEXT:"United States"] and curbs on China's access to advanced foreign technology. That's not to say Beijing doesn't face [USN:L1N46501H TEXT:"challenges"] at home too, with domestic demand stuck in a prolonged slump that has proved stubbornly resistant to stimulus efforts. item.title: Smith & Nephew orthopaedics deal talks with J&J fail over CEO choice, source says
item.description: Smith & Nephew held talks to merge with Johnson & Johnson's orthopaedics division but the discussions collapsed over who would run the enlarged group, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Sabrina Valle
item.content:encoded: Smith & Nephew (SN.L) held talks to merge with Johnson & Johnson's (JNJ.N) orthopaedics division but the discussions collapsed over who would run the enlarged group, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday. British medical devices firm Smith & Nephew and US healthcare conglomerate J&J both declined to comment on an earlier Financial Times report that said the merger talks had been at an advanced stage, with both sides aligned on the main financial terms and structure. The talks fell through at the last minute after Smith & Nephew refused to agree to its former CEO Namal Nawana leading the merged business, the FT report said. According to a person familiar with the matter, J&J was never prepared to pursue a transaction in which Smith & Nephew's Chief Executive Deepak Nath would serve as CEO of the combined company. Smith & Nephew was aware of that position, the person said, but the talks ultimately collapsed after it sought to have Nath lead the merged group. Nawana, who was Smith & Nephew's CEO for 18 months before stepping down in 2019, now heads J&J's orthopaedics division. He was J&J's preferred candidate to lead the combined business, the person added. "The combination would have created a rich portfolio across knee and hip implants, while filling in musculoskeletal gaps in both parties’ offering," said John West, global head of analysis at Mergermarket. Smith & Nephew approached J&J earlier this year with an offer valuing the US company's hip and knee replacement unit at as much as $22 billion, almost double Smith & Nephew's £9.4 billion ($12.58 billion) market value, the person said. J&J announced [USN:L2N3VU0SW TEXT:"plans"] a year ago to separate its orthopaedics business into a standalone company named DePuy Synthes. The unit, which was reportedly seeking a [USN:L4N3ZF1PO TEXT:"$20 billion price tag"], has drawn private equity [USN:L4N4531JY TEXT:"interest"] but no deal has materialised. Last week, J&J said it was leaning toward [USN:L1N45Y0R3 TEXT:"a spinoff of the unit"], with a separation targeted for mid-2027. MANAGEMENT DIRECTION AND TERMS The companies had been eyeing a mid-October announcement before talks ended several weeks ago, the FT said, adding that J&J shareholders would have owned 50.1% of the combined company. Smith & Nephew has been facing weak growth, and after three years of cost cuts and sales initiatives, it is banking on newer products to shore up revenue. Mergermarket's West said it would not be surprising if the companies eventually returned to the negotiating table. ($1 = 0.7470 pounds)

item.title: Stocks fall, but tech shares steady after selloff; oil hits highest in nearly six months
item.description: Major stock indexes ended lower on Friday even as tech shares mostly steadied, while Brent crude oil rose to its highest level in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Valetkevitch, Marc Jones
item.content:encoded: Major stock indexes ended lower on Friday even as tech shares mostly steadied, while Brent crude oil rose to its highest level in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. The Nasdaq eased. European shares also ended lower. An index of semiconductors (.SOX) rose 0.4%. On Thursday, it posted its biggest daily percentage drop since June after a report from Meta Platforms (META.O) reignited worries about the AI trade. The S&P 500 technology index (.SPLRCT) was also up 0.4%. The S&P 500 energy sector (.SPNY) rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia [USN:L1N46903W TEXT:"fanned fears"] over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where United Arab Emirates authorities also reported an oil spill. [USN:L1N46903W TEXT:"Brent crude"] futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 or 3.14%, their highest since April 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80 or 3.8%. Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher. [USN:L6N469158 TEXT:"US Treasury yields"] rose after the benchmark 10-year yield posted on Thursday its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years. "There are still all these headwinds in terms of sticky inflation," said JoAnne Bianco, partner and senior investment strategist at BondBloxx Investment Management in Chicago. The 10-year yield remained under 5% as concerns about the durability of a rally in AI-related stocks lingered. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note was up 3.7 basis points at 4.99%. AI SHARES MIXED Investor focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) , three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street. Meta shares ended down 1%, while Microsoft was up 0.7%. Shares of Alphabet and Amazon eased. "After Meta's report, there's still anxiety over the AI trade to a certain extent," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth in Boston. Investors also digested other corporate earnings news. American Express (AXP.N) shares fell 3.7% after it [USN:L4N4690WS TEXT:"reported"] results and its CEO said the company had good momentum, but needed to become a more "agile and efficient" organization. Telecom company shares, including Verizon (VZ.N) , dropped after a [USN:L4N4682CX TEXT:"report"] that SpaceX (SPCX.O) was in talks with cellular infrastructure companies about launching a US wireless carrier program. The[USN:L6N46917T TEXT:" Dow Jones"] Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34. For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, notching its third straight weekly gain. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) fell 3.96 points, or 0.35%, to 1,118.97. Asia's bourses steadied overnight, with South Korea's KOSPI (.KS11) ending its session higher after shedding as much as 4% earlier. EURO FALLS The euro fell and was down for the week, while euro zone bonds stabilized after recent volatility. The euro has been hit by concerns about unrest in France and the country's budget problems. France [USN:L1N4690GR TEXT:"will deploy"] 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. The euro was last down 0.21% at $1.1191 . [USN:L4N4691FJ TEXT:"European stocks"] recorded their steepest weekly loss since early September. The pan-European STOXX 600 index (.STOXX) fell 0.31% to close at 635.77 points. For the week, the benchmark is down about 1.4%. French yields , which were down 5 basis points at 5.04%, have risen nearly 27 bps this week, the most of any major euro zone country and the most in a week since late May. A selloff in French government bonds this week pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011.

item.title: Apple's foldable iPhone hits stores with $2,000 price tag and scarce supply
item.description: Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Christine Chen, Will Russell
item.content:encoded: Apple's (AAPL.O) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches. From Singapore and Shanghai to London and San Francisco, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days. Competitors such as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones. It is also an early challenge for Apple's new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September. Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary". Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online. In Sydney, where the first Apple store began selling the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT). "This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a 512GB Duo. CEO Ternus played greeter at a store in Austin, Texas, throwing open the doors and high-fiving customers as they streamed in, a video posted on X by CBS Austin showed. A known car enthusiast, Ternus's Austin visit coincides with this weekend's Formula 1 US Grand Prix in the city, with Apple holding exclusive US broadcast and streaming rights to the racing series. At Apple's Fifth Avenue store in New York, marketing head Greg Joswiak opened the doors to a crowd of customers, social media posts showed. Some posts said people had camped outside the store since as early as 4 a.m. local time (0800 GMT). Mohit Chandel, a 32-year-old San Francisco resident and consultant, had promised his father in Singapore an iPhone Duo for his retirement but forgot to pre-order one. So when he spotted a dozen people lining up outside an Apple store around 11 p.m. Thursday, he joined them, ordered a bench and pillow from Walgreens and settled in for the night. "He doesn't know that. All the pre-orders are gone. He's expecting a Duo sometime in the mail so now I have to buy it," Chandel said. In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to [USN:P8N44H02N TEXT:"six straight quarters"] of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices. Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi (1810.HK) , but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6 a.m. for Apple's first foldable. "I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said. Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models. Others were resellers. In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked. Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain. "Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said. MIXED REVIEWS Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers. But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple customers. "It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber. Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone." In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one. "I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices." TOUGH TO FIND Apple's entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC. IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast. "Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo. "Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said. ($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars) ($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

item.title: Marvel's gem-studded Infinity Gauntlet replica heads to auction in Abu Dhabi
item.description: A replica of the Infinity Gauntlet, the powerful artifact featured in Marvel Comics and Marvel films, will go up for auction on December 8 in Abu Dhabi, Julien's Auctions and East Continental Gems said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Danielle Broadway, Matt Silverstein
item.content:encoded: A replica of the Infinity Gauntlet, the powerful artifact featured in Marvel Comics and Marvel films, will go up for auction on December 8 in Abu Dhabi, Julien's Auctions and East Continental Gems said on Thursday. The oversized glove, embedded with six gemstones representing the Infinity Stones, was made famous in the 2018 film "Avengers: Infinity War," in which the purple villain Thanos uses the gauntlet to wipe out half of all life with a snap of his fingers. Infinity Stones are six supercharged gems that control essential aspects of existence in Marvel lore: Space, Mind, Soul, Reality, Power and Time. The Marvel Cinematic Universe depicts a multiversal world through superhero films and television series featuring characters including Spider-Man, Iron Man, Hulk and Scarlet Witch. "You can buy it because you are a lover, a passionate fan of Marvel," Talia Friedman, who leads special projects for Julien's Auctions, told Reuters on Wednesday. "You can love it because you are a passionate jewelry collector. You can love it because you want the trophy," she added, noting the item, which will be auctioned at Rosewood Abu Dhabi and displayed in Bahrain, could appeal to both comic book fans and art collectors. The replica, created by East Continental Gems, contains six real gemstones: a ruby, garnet, sapphire, amethyst, emerald and yellow diamond. Each gemstone represents one of the Infinity Stones. The December sale comes as Disney's Marvel franchise prepares for the release of the high-budget film "Avengers: Doomsday," which arrives in theaters on December 18.

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: Wall Street finit dans le rouge une semaine mouvementée autour de l'IA
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Wall Street finit dans le rouge une semaine mouvementée autour de l'IA PARIS, 23 octobre (Reuters) - La Bourse de New York a fini en baisse vendredi, au terme d'une semaine mouvementée pour le secteur de l'intelligence artificielle (IA) alors que les investisseurs ont désormais les yeux rivés sur de nouveaux résultats d'entreprises et la décision prochaine de politique monétaire de la Réserve fédérale américaine (Fed). L'Europe finit dans le rouge, la France attend le verdict de Moody's 23 octobre (Reuters) - Les Bourses européennes ont terminé en baisse vendredi, dans un climat peu favorable aux actions, les cours du pétrole grimpant à nouveau et les finances publiques françaises suscitant de plus en plus de méfiance alors que Moody's doit actualiser la note de crédit de la deuxième économie de la zone euro. États-Unis: Le moral des ménages se dégrade moins que prévu en octobre, selon une enquête de l'Université du Michigan 23 octobre (Reuters) - Le moral des ménages américains s'est dégradé moins que prévu en octobre, montrent vendredi les résultats définitifs de l'enquête mensuelle de l'Université du Michigan. Moody's maintient la note souveraine de la France à "Aa3" PARIS, 23 octobre (Reuters) - L'agence de notation Moody's a décidé vendredi de maintenir la note de crédit de la France à "Aa3", assortie d'une perspective négative, alors que la plupart des analystes s'attendaient à une dégradation à "A1". Stellantis, Bolt et Grand Paris veulent lancer des services de mobilité autonome dès 2028 23 octobre (Reuters) - Stellantis, l'entreprise estonienne de VTC Bolt et la région Île-de-France prévoient de lancer un programme de conduite autonome dans la capitale française en 2028, en utilisant des véhicules du constructeur franco-italo-américain, ont-elles annoncé vendredi dans un communiqué commun. La Royaume-Uni recommande à la population d'avoir des réserves d'urgence pour trois jours LONDRES, 23 octobre (Reuters) - Le gouvernement britannique a conseillé vendredi à la population de disposer chez elle de réserves d'urgence pour trois jours, une recommandation qui, selon lui, a été renforcée par le bug logiciel PHP de cette semaine, ainsi que par un été record marqué par la canicule, la sécheresse et les incendies de forêt. AmEx relève son objectif de bénéfice grâce aux dépenses de sa clientèle aisée 23 octobre (Reuters) - American Express (AmEx) a relevé vendredi son objectif de bénéfice pour 2026 après avoir publié de solides résultats au troisième trimestre de son exercice, tirés, une fois de plus, par les dépenses des clients fortunés. L'Oréal grimpe, la croissance au T3 illustre la résilience des cosmétiques 23 octobre (Reuters) - L'action L'Oréal était en nette hausse vendredi en milieu de matinée, le géant français des cosmétiques ayant publié la veille une croissance des ventes trimestrielles supérieure aux attentes, soulignant sa résilience dans un contexte de ralentissement du reste du secteur du luxe. Volkswagen-Les salariés menacent de faire grève si les accords ne sont pas respectés FRANCFORT, 23 octobre (Reuters) - Les dirigeants syndicaux allemands ont menacé d'organiser des grèves chez Volkswagen à partir de janvier, si l'entreprise ne revient pas d'ici fin octobre sur sa récente annulation des accords salariaux, marquant ainsi une escalade des conflits sociaux au sein du groupe. Kering chute de 10% après un nouveau recul des ventes de Gucci 23 octobre (Reuters) - L'action Kering dévisse de 10% vendredi, au lendemain des résultats trimestriels du géant français du luxe, marqués par une baisse des ventes de Gucci, sa marque phare, dans un contexte de faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins.
